destination.name: The Faroe Islands
destination.pitch: Eighteen islands of wet green rock where the walking is the trip and the forecast rewrites the plan every morning.

because.nature: Sea cliffs, gorges and waterfalls sit within twenty minutes of almost every road you drive.
because.exploration: Six or seven villages a day is realistic and most of them hold under fifty people.
because.food: Three or four serious kitchens exist, all in Tórshavn, and they are booked out weeks ahead.
because.relaxation: Evenings offer eating and sleeping and nothing else, which some people count as rest.
because.culture: Turf-roofed churches, a language with 50,000 speakers, and a rowing boat hung in a church as a war memorial.
because.adventure: Exposed ridges, a compulsory guide on Mykines, and a boat timetable that owns your day.
because.city: Tórshavn holds 14,000 people and you will have walked all of it in one afternoon.

destination.caveat: The weather decides the itinerary, not you: reckon on losing two of seven days to sideways rain and cloud sitting on every summit, and the Mykines ferry gets cancelled on swell with no notice and no second chance that week. Put together for you just now from what I know, rather than checked against today's opening times. Worth confirming anything you're pinning the trip on.

cities.name: Tórshavn
cities.base: The old town at Tinganes and Reyn, because the four restaurants worth booking are a four-minute walk from bed and parking anywhere else is pointless.

cities.name: Vágar
cities.base: Sørvágur or Miðvágur, ten minutes from the airport and five from the Mykines ferry berth, which is the only reason to sleep here.

cities.name: Gjógv
cities.base: Gjáargarður at the top of the village, which is effectively the only bed in Gjógv and the only kitchen too.

cities.name: Klaksvík
cities.base: The harbour end near Klaksvíksvegur, walking distance from the Kalsoy ferry berth so you can be on the first boat.

cities.name: Saksun and north Streymoy
cities.base: No beds worth the name here, so it is a half day out of Tórshavn or Gjógv and back.

cities.name: Mykines
cities.base: One guesthouse and a season that runs May to August, so treat it as a day off the Sørvágur boat and do not plan to sleep there.

outings.name: the Sørvágsvatn lake walk
outings.why: Flat lakeside track for an hour, then a short climb to Trælanípa where the lake appears to hang above the Atlantic; the ground is boggy all year and the landowner charges 200 DKK a head at a staffed gate.
outings.season: All year, gate normally staffed 09:00 to 17:00, guided depar
outings.fallback: Walk the lake shore for thirty minutes and turn back before the climb.

outings.name: Múlafossur and the Gásadalur road
outings.why: The drive past Bøur and Tindhólmur, through the 2004 tunnel, to a waterfall that falls off the cliff below the village; five minutes of walking and a lot of wind.
outings.fallback: Stay in the car at the upper viewpoint and drive back down.

outings.name: Mykines and the lighthouse walk
outings.why: Forty-five minutes on the Jósup, then the puffin slopes, the footbridge and the 1909 lighthouse at the far west end; a guide is compulsory past the village and the whole thing is off if there is swell.
outings.season: 1 May to 31 August for the daily ferry and the puffins
outings.fallback: If the boat is cancelled, drive Bøur, Gásadalur and Sandavágur instead and eat the loss.

outings.name: Kallur lighthouse on Kalsoy
outings.why: Ferry from Klaksvík, single-lane tunnels the length of the island to Trøllanes, then forty-five minutes up grass to a small light on a knife-edge headland; the drop either side is real.
outings.season: All year, though the ferry thins badly outside summer
outings.fallback: Stop at Mikladalur for the seal woman statue and take the next boat back.

outings.name: Slættaratindur from the Eiði road
outings.why: 880 m, the highest point in the country, straight up from the road pass with no scrambling; the summit is in cloud more days than not, so go the morning it is clear rather than the day you planned.
outings.fallback: Drive the pass down the hairpins to Funningur and walk the village.

outings.name: the Gjógv gorge and Ambadalur
outings.why: Down the wooden stairs into the natural harbour cleft, then a grass path along the cliff tops to look back at the Búgvin stack; 50 DKK in an honesty box at the gate.
outings.season: All year, though the stairs are slick after rain
outings.fallback: The gorge stairs alone, forty minutes.

outings.name: Saksun and Tjørnuvík
outings.why: The sanded-up lagoon at Saksun on a falling tide, then Fossá and the black beach at Tjørnuvík; the Saksun walk is 75 DKK per person at a card gate and the tide, not the weather, sets the hour you leave.
outings.season: All year, low tide only for the lagoon
outings.fallback: Saksun church and the valley viewpoint, then straight on to Tjørnuvík.

outings.name: Drangarnir
outings.why: Guided only, on private land, to the sea arch between Vágar and Tindhólmur; three days a week and around 550 to 600 DKK a head, which is the single most expensive half day in the country.
outings.season: 1 April to 1 October, Wednesdays, Saturdays and Sundays at 1
outings.fallback: Look at Tindhólmur from the Bøur road for nothing.

outings.name: Kirkjubøur and the old road over Kirkjubøreyn
outings.why: The 6 km cairned path the villagers used before the road, over the ridge and down to the unfinished Magnus Cathedral and the oldest inhabited wooden house in Europe; navigation is easy in clear air and unpleasant in fog.
outings.season: May to September for the walk, all year for the village
outings.fallback: Drive the 11 km, see the cathedral shell and Roykstovan, drive back.

outings.name: Villingadalsfjall from Viðareiði
outings.why: 844 m of steep grass straight off the village for the northernmost view in the islands; 200 DKK in the honesty box, and the Enniberg cliff beyond needs a guide and a genuinely dry day.
outings.fallback: Walk the Viðareiði shore to the 1892 church and back.

outings.name: the Vestmanna bird cliffs boat
outings.why: Two hours under 600 m cliffs in an open boat; it is cancelled on swell about as often as it sails, and the birds are easier to see for free from the Vágar roads.
outings.fallback: Drive to Vestmanna, look up the fjord from the quay, drive back.

outings.name: Nólsoy on the evening ferry
outings.why: Twenty minutes across the sound to a one-street island with a pub and 50,000 pairs of storm petrels; the petrel walk runs at night in summer and needs booking with a local guide.
outings.season: All year for the ferry, June to August for the storm petrels
outings.fallback: Walk Tórshavn's old lanes at Reyn instead.

places.name: Tinganes
places.note: The government still works out of these red turf-roofed sheds on the harbour spit, so you walk through a working office quarter in ten minutes.

places.name: Skansin
places.note: A 1580 fort with British naval guns left from the 1940 occupation and the best free look down over the harbour.

places.name: Tjóðsavnið
places.note: Viking finds, the carved Kirkjubøur pews and a boat hall; daily 10:00 to 17:00 from 1 May to 30 September, Thursday to Sunday 13:00 to 17:00 the rest of the year.

places.name: Listasavn Føroya
places.note: The national gallery in the town plantation, shut Mondays, and the correct move on the day the cloud sits at fifty metres.

places.name: Norðurlandahúsið
places.note: Grass-roofed Nordic culture house with a café and a concert board; check what is on the night you land, because it is the only reliable live music outside summer.

places.name: Kirkjubøur: Múrurin and Kirkjubøargarður
places.note: An unfinished 14th-century cathedral shell and an 11th-century farmhouse one family has held for seventeen generations; 150 DKK covers both, St Olav's church next door is free.

places.name: Nólsoy village and the Tórshavn ferry
places.note: Twenty minutes across the sound to one street, one pub and the world's largest storm petrel colony; check the last sailing before you go, it is early.

places.name: Barbara Fish House
places.note: Fish tapas in a turf-roofed house in the old lanes, Monday to Saturday from six, and it seats so few that a fortnight's notice is not enough in July.

places.name: Ræst
places.note: Everything is fermented, including the lamb and the fish, and you will know by the second course whether this trip includes a second visit; ring to confirm the week's opening, it varies.

places.name: ROKS
places.note: The KOKS family's seafood room on the harbour, Tuesday to Sunday from six, and far easier to book than KOKS itself out at Leynavatn.

places.name: Áarstova
places.note: Slow-cooked Faroese lamb in a black timber house, open seven nights, which in a town where most kitchens shut two days a week is worth a lot.

places.name: Cafe Natúr
places.note: Old wooden pub on the harbour front with Föroya Bjór on tap and live music some weekends; it is where the town actually drinks.

places.name: Trælanípa and the Sørvágsvatn lake walk
places.note: Flat boggy track along the lake then a climb to the cliff where the water looks like it floats above the sea; 200 DKK a head unguided at the staffed gate, 450 DKK with the guide and a hot drink.

places.name: Bøsdalafossur
places.note: The lake tips straight off the rock into the Atlantic here; twenty minutes further on the same ticket as Trælanípa, so do not turn back early.

places.name: Múlafossur
places.note: The waterfall off the cliff below the village, five minutes from the car park, and it does live up to the photographs unless the wind is blowing the water back up the cliff.

places.name: Gásadalur village
places.note: About sixteen people live here and they had no road until the tunnel opened in 2004; walk the lane, stay out of the gardens, people are at home.

places.name: Bøur
places.note: Turf roofs, a small white church and the head-on view of Tindhólmur across the fjord; ten cars fill the pull-in, so stop on the way out rather than the way in.

places.name: Tindhólmur viewpoint
places.note: The five-peaked islet in Sørvágsfjørður, uninhabited and privately owned; you look at it from the road, and landing needs a licensed boat and a guide.

places.name: Drangarnir
places.note: Guided access only, Wednesdays, Saturdays and Sundays at 11:00 and 13:00 between 1 April and 1 October, 550 to 600 DKK a head; book before you fly, the groups are capped.

places.name: Sandavágur Church
places.note: Red-roofed church from 1917 holding the 13th-century runestone that names Torkil Onundarson as the first settler here; the door is often locked outside service times.

places.name: Trøllkonufingur
places.note: A 313 m sea stack at the end of a short boggy path from Sandavágur; the walk is easy, the stack itself has been climbed about twice and is not an option.

places.name: Sørvágur harbour
places.note: Where the Jósup leaves for Mykines; read the board here the evening before, because swell cancels the crossing far more often than rain does.

places.name: Gásadalsgarður
places.note: Soup, lamb and cake in the village guesthouse, and the only food between the tunnel and Sørvágur; summer opening, and ring ahead in shoulder season.

places.name: Fiskastykkið
places.note: Seafood in a converted fish factory by the water at Miðvágur, and the only proper dinner on Vágar; the week is short and the season shorter, so confirm by phone.

places.name: the Jósup crossing to Mykines
places.note: Forty-five minutes each way: daily at 09:30, 13:30 and 17:30 from 1 May to 31 August, but Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday only at 10:45 in April and from 1 September to 8 October, and you board by stepping across a gap onto a moving deck.

places.name: Mykines village
places.note: A handful of turf-roofed houses on a green shelf above the landing; the village takes twenty minutes and everything else on the island is uphill from it.

places.name: the puffin slopes above Lambi
places.note: Burrows a metre from the path from mid-May to late August and empty cliffs the rest of the year; the 250 DKK hiking fee is separate from the ferry, a guide is compulsory past the village, and a combined ticket runs about 400 DKK booked online.

places.name: the Mykineshólmur footbridge
places.note: A 40 m span over a gorge to the islet, fenced and structurally fine; it is also the point where the wind hits hardest and people turn round.

places.name: Mykineshólmur lighthouse
places.note: The 1909 light at the western end of the country, about ninety minutes each way from the village, and the turnaround time is set by the ferry rather than by you.

places.name: the gannet colony at Hólmgjógv
places.note: The only gannetry in the Faroe Islands, loud and smelly and visible straight off the lighthouse path.

places.name: Mykines Church
places.note: Small wooden church from 1879 in the middle of the village, usually open in summer and locked out of season.

places.name: Kristianshús
places.note: The guesthouse kitchen is the only food on the island, soup and cake and not much else; carry a packed lunch anyway, because it closes when the season does.

places.name: Knúkur
places.note: The 560 m ridge above the village, steep and fully exposed, and in cloud most days; skip it if you also want the lighthouse on one ferry day.

places.name: the Gjógv sea gorge
places.note: A 200 m cleft in the cliff that served as the village harbour, with a winch and wooden stairs still in place; the steps are slick for hours after rain.

places.name: the Ambadalur headland walk
places.note: Grass path along the cliff tops to look back at the Búgvin stack; the landowner asks 50 DKK per adult in an honesty box at the gate and it is worth paying.

places.name: Gjáargarður
places.note: The guesthouse dining room is the only kitchen in Gjógv; say at breakfast that you want dinner, because they cook to a headcount and will not feed a walk-in at eight.

places.name: Slættaratindur
places.note: 880 m and the highest point in the country, straight up from the road pass with no scrambling; the top is in cloud most days, so take the clear morning when it comes rather than the day you booked.

places.name: Funningur Church
places.note: Turf-roofed wooden church from 1847 at the water's edge; the hairpin descent from the pass is half the reason to come.

places.name: Risin og Kellingin from Eiði
places.note: The giant and the witch, two stacks off the north cape, seen best from the old clifftop football pitch above Eiði.

places.name: Elduvík
places.note: About twenty houses at the end of a fjord road, a stream running through the middle and almost no one there; the best free hour on Eysturoy.

places.name: Rinkusteinar at Oyndarfjørður
places.note: Two boulders in the shallows said to rock with the swell; they barely move, the viewing platform is a long way round, and the detour costs an hour you need elsewhere.

places.name: Blásastova at Norðragøta
places.note: A black turf-roofed merchant's house kept as a village museum; summer opening and short afternoon hours, so check locally before you drive down.

places.name: Fuglafjørður harbour and Varmakelda
places.note: A working fishing town with the only warm spring in the islands just outside it; the spring is lukewarm and dull, the quay at unloading time is not.

places.name: Christianskirkjan
places.note: A 1963 church built like a Norse hall, with an eight-oar boat from Viðareiði hung from the roof as a memorial to sailors lost in the war; opening hours are short and posted on the door.

places.name: Föroya Bjór
places.note: The national brewery since 1888; tours run by prior arrangement rather than on a public timetable, so email before you drive up the fjord.

places.name: Fríða Kaffihús
places.note: Soup, cake and the best coffee north of Tórshavn, Monday to Saturday 10:00 to 19:00 and shut Sundays; twenty seats inside, so book if there are more than four of you.

places.name: Klaksvík harbour walk
places.note: A deep-water fishing port squeezed between two fjords; walk the quay while a boat is unloading and you see what actually pays for this country.

places.name: Klakkur
places.note: 413 m on a clear gravel track from the top of town, ninety minutes up, and the best view of the Northern Isles for no money and no permission.

places.name: Viðareiði
places.note: The northernmost village, reached on a road cut under the cliffs, with an 1892 church holding silver given by the British crown after a local rescue.

places.name: Villingadalsfjall
places.note: 844 m of steep grass straight off the village, 200 DKK in an honesty box at the gate; the Enniberg cliff beyond it is guided only and not a casual add-on.

places.name: Kunoy village and the plantation
places.note: One of the very few stands of trees in the whole country, planted in a sheltered bowl behind the village, and reached through an unlit single-lane tunnel.

places.name: the Sam ferry to Syðradalur
places.note: Twenty minutes to Kalsoy, with eight sailings on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays and fewer on other days; the boat takes twelve cars, so in summer leave yours in Klaksvík and use the island bus.

places.name: Kallur lighthouse
places.note: Forty-five minutes up from Trøllanes to a small light on a narrow headland, 200 DKK per adult at the gate; the ground falls away on both sides and it is no place to be in wind.

places.name: Kópakonan at Mikladalur
places.note: The seal woman in bronze on the rocks below the village, down a long flight of steps, with the curse she pronounced written on a board at the top.

places.name: Trøllanes
places.note: A dozen people at the far end of four single-lane tunnels; it is the trailhead for Kallur and there is nowhere to buy food, fuel or a coffee.

places.name: Pollurin, the Saksun lagoon
places.note: A sea inlet that a storm sanded shut, walkable out to the sea gap at low tide only; 75 DKK per person by card at an unmanned gate, and people do get cut off by the incoming tide every summer.

places.name: Saksun Church
places.note: Small turf-roofed church that was taken apart in Tjørnuvík in 1858, carried over the mountain and rebuilt here; stand outside it, the farm around it is private.

places.name: Dúvugarðar
places.note: A 17th-century farmhouse kept as a museum on a farm that still runs about 700 ewes; summer opening only and the hours move year to year, so ring Tjóðsavnið first.

places.name: Tjørnuvík
places.note: Black sand beach at the end of a dead-end road, surfers in the water most weekends, and a clean line of sight out to Risin og Kellingin.

places.name: Fossá
places.note: The tallest waterfall in the islands, dropping in two steps right beside the road; you can scramble to the middle shelf in ten minutes and get soaked doing it.

places.name: Haldarsvík Church
places.note: The only octagonal church in the country, with a Last Supper on the altar wall painted using local villagers as the apostles.

places.name: Hvalvík Church
places.note: The oldest surviving wooden church in the Faroe Islands, built in 1829, turf on the roof and the door usually unlocked in daylight.

places.name: Kvívík Viking ruins
places.note: Stone foundations of a Viking longhouse and byre on the shore, fenced, free and about ten minutes of your day, half of which is the walk down.

places.name: the Vestmanna bird cliffs boat
places.note: Two hours in an open boat under 600 m cliffs for about 500 DKK, cancelled on swell roughly as often as it sails, and you will see more birds for nothing from the Vágar roads or on Mykines.
